How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

This is version 3 (last modification 2026-10-26) of our preprint published on PsyArXiv at https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/r259d_v3. All materials (reproducible manuscript, analysis code, datasets, codebooks, questionnaires) are available in the project's repository on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at https://osf.io/p7492/. A Quarto Manuscript website is hosted at https://florianpargent.github.io/gold-standard-items/ florianpargent.github.io/gold-standard-items/. The data have previously been analyzed in the dissertation thesis of the first author at https://doi.org/10.5282/edoc.23628. As part of the dissertation, a preregistration was published at https://osf.io/cz3uv/?view_only=9cac02db231b48629fea9ae53c3038b9 that differs from the analyses reported in the current manuscript. The

Evaluating Psychological Scales with Gold-Standard Items: Lessons from Measures of Body Height, Weight, and Age

Psychological researchers spend a lot of time developing questionnaires, called psychological scales, and use latent variable modeling to test whether their scales measure the intended psychological construct (Holt et al., 2010). When constructing items for a new scale, the common approach is to first carefully define the construct or latent variable to be measured, and then generate indicators for it based on this definition (see Anastasi & Urbina, 1997). When based on common factor analytic test models in which each item is an indicator of only one latent variable, items are theoretically interchangeable with respect to their latent variable; that means they all measure the same construct. In theory, the item selection is considered content valid if the items represent a random selection of all possible items that could be used to measure the latent variable. However, in many cases, the item pool is unknown, so it is not possible to select items at random. Thus, in practice, when items are not sampled randomly, a scale is considered content valid only if each aspect of the construct definition is reflected by at least one item. The items of a scale are then used together to measure the latent variable. When evaluating such a scale empirically, an important goal is to assess whether the questionnaire actually measures the intended construct. While standard practices report model fit indices and evaluate whether each item has a substantial response variance and item loading, this does not directly answer the question of what the items actually measure. And even if researchers go the extra mile and reason about the items by interpreting the observed pattern of item loadings (i.e., which items have relatively higher loadings), they often lack a clear strategy for what to compare them to and which patterns would suggest that the items measure the construct as intended. In the most widely applied test-theoretic models (e.g., factor analytic models), item loadings are interpreted as the extent to which items correlate with, and thus measure, their latent variable (see Lord et al., 1968). Would it not be great if we had at least one indicator with a strong theoretical justification that this gold-standard item is a particularly good measure of the latent variable?

Then we could include the gold-standard item as an additional indicator in the questionnaire's evaluation and check whether it has the highest, or at least a very high, loading among the items used to measure the latent variable. If other items load substantially higher than the goldstandard item, one might rightly question whether the scale measures the construct as originally intended, and could start investigating the actual meaning of the latent variable by making sense of the complete loading pattern.

In this study, we examine the idea of evaluating psychological scales with gold-standard items by constructing three psychological questionnaires for the physical traits of body height, body weight, and chronological age. Extending previous examples of psychological measures of body height (Bortolotti et al., 2013; Hilbert et al., 2022; Van der Linden, 2016), we chose these physical traits because, unlike psychological latent variables, they can be directly assessed using valid gold-standard items in the form of numerical self-reports of the respective physical trait (e.g., self-reported body height in centimeters). We derive and evaluate three assumptions that we argue should hold in our idealized setting with theoretically strong gold-standard items, assuming that our psychological scales achieved valid measurements of the respective latent variables. To reduce the risk of confounding our findings by how we constructed our psychological scales, we adhere to best practices in the literature on scale construction and item wording. We also compare questionnaire versions with two different response formats as an additional robustness check. After presenting our analyses, we discuss the implementation of gold-standard items for evaluating psychological scales for more common psychological constructs. Furthermore, we discuss the overlap between gold-standard items and single-item measures, which are becoming increasingly common in applied psychological research (Allen et al., 2022).

Theoretical Background

Gold-Standard Items for Physical Traits

The idea to construct psychological scales for physical traits is not new: To illustrate the usefulness of logistic item response models, Van der Linden (2016) analyzed a teaching dataset from the Netherlands in which body height was measured based on items with two response categories (e.g., "I bump my head quite often.", p. 27). He notes that this approach is unusual, as body height appears to be a physical variable that can only be measured using a yardstick.

However, he argues that because differences in height do influence behavior, it is plausible to treat such behavioral indicators as proxies for body height and use them to construct a psychological scale of height. As the author himself noted, a limitation of his dataset was that it did not include a physical height measurement for comparison.

In contrast, Bortolotti et al. (2013) compared psychological and physical measurements to demonstrate the validity of psychological measurements and the practical utility of psychological measurement models. They also constructed a 27-item scale to assess body height using a binary response format. Participants from Brazil were asked to respond to items such as "Do I think I would do well in a basketball team?" (Bortolotti et al., 2013 (Bortolotti et al., , p. 2350)). At the end of the scale, participants also indicated their actual height in centimeters, a self-reported physical gold-standard item. Bortolotti et al. compared the parameters estimated from the latent variable body height with the response on the gold-standard item. Their analyses revealed a strong correlation of .86 between self-reported physical height and the estimated person parameter derived from a two-parameter logistic model of the psychological scale. However, the reported analyses do not establish whether the self-reported physical height item would have had the highest standardized loading in a model including both this item and the questionnaire items (Bortolotti et al., 2013).

Although both studies concluded that their scales successfully measured physical body height, they also identified some items that did not fit the one-dimensional model well, had extreme item difficulties, or did not have a linear relationship with self-reported physical height.

These findings show that even for a relatively simple trait such as physical body height, it is not trivial to construct appropriate items. In particular, the examples of item misfit in Van der Linden (2016) suggest that, in addition to physical height, the items also measured a psychological representation of body height, but the author did not further investigate possible interpretations for this residual psychological component.

Item Wording

One important aspect of item construction is item wording. Surprisingly, Pargent et al.

(2019) and Goretzko et al. (2020) showed that the quality of item wording did not, in fact, impact model fit based on commonly used fit indices in confirmatory factor analysis. However, clear wording is indisputably essential for understanding an item correctly, highlighting the boundaries of fit indices and emphasizing the importance of conducting cognitive interviews with individuals from the target population when developing items for a new scale (Gehlbach & Brinkworth, 2011; Willis, 2005; Willis & Artino, 2013). If a person does not understand an item correctly, their response can never be valid, regardless of any model fit indices (for an extreme but illustrative example, see Maul, 2017). Thus, it seems problematic to evaluate the quality of a questionnaire solely by looking at the fit of the latent variable model, item loadings, or reliability estimates. In this context, McNeish et al. (2018) stated that fit indices (e.g., Root Mean Square Error of Approximation, RMSEA; Standardized Root Mean Square Residual, SRMR; and the Comparative Fit Index, CFI) should always be considered in combination with measurement quality (i.e., reliability) and the size of standardized factor loadings. Gold-standard items offer an additional systematic strategy for scale validation by using the pattern of factor loadings to provide a reference point for evaluating the meaning of other items.

Response Format

An important topic that hinders the generalization of methodological insights across questionnaires is the potential effect of response formats on scale quality. Hilbert et al. (2016) presented initial evidence that different response formats might not measure the same latent variable. They found that the correlation between latent variables measured by identically worded items ranged from .76 to .88 when using scales with two versus five response categories, as well as a visual analogue scale. The question arises: Which of these questionnaires best measures the intended construct?

What we do know in this context is how the number of response categories affects reliability estimates, because a vast body of literature has compared different numbers of response categories for rating-scale items. We cite several exemplary studies to demonstrate how complex and difficult it is to choose an optimal number of response categories and to highlight what we can conclude from their results. First, Preston and Colman (2000) reported that two response categories had the lowest retest reliability and relatively poor validity and discriminative power. They recommended applying rating scales with at least seven response categories. In contrast, Lee and Paek (2014, p. 663) concluded that "caution should be made if a scale has only two response categories, but that limitation may be overcome by manipulating other scale features, namely, scale length or item discrimination". Weijters et al. (2010) recommend rating scales with five fully labeled response categories for samples drawn from the general population. In their recommendations, the authors considered an extreme response style, responses to reversed items, and acquiescence. However, Masuda et al. (2017) found that persons with low motivation tend to use the middle category, implying that a middle category is not advisable. Similarly, Bradley et al. (2015, p. 8) concluded from their study that "for constructing measures from survey responses, the inclusion of a neutral middle category distorts the data to the point where it is not possible to construct meaningful measures." Simms et al. (2019) suggest that researchers concerned about the ambiguity of a middle category can use six response categories, as their study found no further gains in psychometric precision beyond six categories.

All in all, the reviewed literature suggests that to achieve high reliability, seven response categories might be slightly favored, but there is also evidence to omit the middle category due to its inconsistent use.

The Present Study

We quote from a review on the application of item response models and factor analysis (Holt et al., 2010, p. 288): "In our opinion, researchers could take far better advantage of their theoretical knowledge and/or expectations by incorporating their a priori knowledge of the items and scales in the analyses. This should be reflected 1) by a more frequent application of confirmatory techniques, especially in the construction of new scales, and 2) by adding interpretability of factors and item contents to the criteria used for model evaluation." In line with this statement and the aforementioned research and recommendations, we assess three physical traits to replicate and extend previous findings. First, we constructed scales for body height, body weight, and age. Second, we used items with two response categories to replicate the results for body height reported by Bortolotti et al. (2013). Third, we applied an additional format with six response categories, omitting the middle category, which is often overused by respondents with low motivation (e.g., see Masuda et al., 2017). We aimed to investigate whether the results of Bortolotti et al. (2013) hold true for body height and other physical traits, and whether we can identify a residual psychological component in self-report questionnaires of physical traits, as indicated by Van der Linden (2016). Further, we investigate whether the main results are robust across response formats and whether the majority view in the literature is correct in assuming that items with six response categories have higher reliability and, possibly, better validity than items with two response categories (Lee & Paek, 2014; Preston & Colman, 2000; Weijters et al., 2010). In more detail, we argue that if our new scales measure their respective physical trait as intended, we expect to observe the following patterns: • Assumption 1: The gold-standard items (self-reported physical body height, body weight, and age) should have the highest or at least one of the highest factor loadings among other questionnaire items measuring the respective physical trait (because in one-factor measurement models, a standardized loading can be interpreted as the correlation between the latent variable and the item).

• Assumption 2: Even if gold-standard items have the highest factor loading (and especially if Assumption 1 does not hold), the measurement of physical traits with questionnaire items possibly captures an additional component that can be interpreted as a psychological representation of the physical trait. When item responses are predicted by the gold-standard item and gender (as we would expect gender differences in self-perception, see McCreary, 2002), there should remain systematic variance that can be explained by a common latent variable. Ideally, the loading pattern on this residual latent variable should be interpretable to identify the meaning of the psychological component.

• Assumption 3a, b: The correlation pattern among the latent variables of the physical traits (in a three-factor model with correlated latent variables) should closely correspond to the correlations among the gold-standard items (3a). For scales with six response categories, reliability estimates should be higher, and correlations among latent variables and among goldstandard items should be more closely aligned than for scales with two response categories (3b).

Methods

All materials (reproducible manuscript, analysis code, datasets, codebooks, questionnaires) for this manuscript are openly available on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at https://osf.io/p7492/ (Eichhorn et al., 2025). A Quarto Manuscripts website presenting the manuscript and electronic supplementary materials is hosted at https://florianpargent.github.io/gold-standard-items/.

Scale Construction

Initial Item Pool

First, we constructed items for the physical traits of body height, body weight, and age.

Age was defined as chronological age in years, corresponding to the time elapsed since a person's birth (Montepare & Lachman, 1989; Schwall, 2012). Height was defined as the height of an upright person from the sole of the foot to the top of the head in centimeters, and body weight as the physical mass of a person in kilograms (Martin, 1929). The initial items were developed by 124 psychology students (through deductive item construction, Burisch, 1984) and 24 persons (through a prototype approach, see Broughton, 1984) who deviated from the German population mean by at least one standard deviation in the relevant characteristics (separately for women and men). The 24 persons with extreme trait expressions were asked to think of prototypical behaviors for each construct to assess the whole spectrum of the latent variable. This process resulted in an initial set of 138 items (response categories were not yet tested here).

Cognitive Interviews

In a second step, we examined how these items were interpreted and whether they were connected to additional concepts unrelated to the constructs using cognitive interviews. We conducted interviews lasting two to three hours and applied various cognitive procedures, including probing, paraphrasing, concurrent think-aloud, and retrospective think-aloud (Prüfer & Rexroth, 1996 , 2005). The literature on cognitive interviews recommends five to 30 interviews but indicates that the most serious problems in item wording can already be identified with a small number of interviews (Willis, 2005; Willis & Artino, 2013). The interviews were conducted with 8 people (4 women and 4 men) aged between 21 and 77 (M = 44.50, SD = 20.78). The level of education ranged from a high school diploma to a university degree. After the cognitive interviews, misleading items were reformulated or eliminated (Faulbaum et al., 2009), resulting in 61 remaining items.

Pilot Study

In a third step, these 61 items were pilot-tested online with a new sample of initially 456 people. However, we excluded 66 subjects who had not completed the questionnaire, resulting in a sample of 390 participants aged between 18 and 77 years (M = 31.91, SD = 12.82), including 302 women (77.44%) and 88 men (22.56%). The level of education was distributed as follows: 0% no school-leaving certificate, 3.33% secondary school-leaving certificate/elementary school or equivalent, 17.18% secondary school or equivalent, 35.90% vocational baccalaureate or high school diploma, 40.77% college degree or university degree, 2.82% doctorate or habilitation. Of all respondents, 95.38% stated German as their native language. Based on these survey responses, we excluded items if a) their highest loading was not on the intended factor in threedimensional exploratory factor analyses, b) their main and secondary loadings were nearly equal, or c) their main loading was less than or equal to .30. Additionally, if (d) items had very similar content, items with lower loadings were excluded. More details on the item construction process can be found in Eichhorn (2019). We recomputed the exploratory factor analyses, item total correlations, and reliability estimates that were computed in this final item selection stage and report them in our electronic supplementary materials (ESM C).

No power analysis was performed to determine the sample size of the pilot study. Instead, the goal was to collect data from approximately 150 subjects. No data was analyzed before data collection ended.

Final Scales

Based on these criteria, 12 final items were selected for each physical trait (see Appendix A). 1 For each of the three questionnaires, we created two versions for our main studyone with two response categories combining verbal labels ("does not apply" and "applies") with numeric anchors (numbers 0 and 1) and one with six response categories combining verbal endpoints ("does not apply" to "applies", only endpoints were labeled) with full numeric anchoring (numbers from 1 to 6). The two-category scale version was included because we wanted to replicate the results by Bortolotti et al. (2013) and Van der Linden (2016), who also used a binary response format, and because this response format is commonly used in clinical assessment (Clark & Watson, 2019; Rosellini & Brown, 2021). The six-category scale version was used as a robustness check to ensure that our results hold for ordinal response formats, which are common in practice, and to replicate the common finding that reliability estimates are higher for scales with more than two response categories (Preston & Colman, 2000). Using six response categories is an obvious synthesis of the literature, favoring a higher number of response categories (Preston & Colman, 2000) whilst avoiding a middle category (Masuda et al., 2017), and there is also empirical support that six categories are a good choice (Simms et al., 2019). However, we acknowledge that the evidence is not clear-cut, and other researchers recommend five or seven response categories, depending on the study population and purpose 1 Because the described procedure did not return at least 12 items for all scales, the decision was made to keep two weight items (W3 and W7) and two age items (A7 and A10) with very similar content. Compared to the pilot study, one height item (H7) and one weight item (W7) were slightly rephrased to simplify the wording and reduce similarities in sentence structure with other items in the scale. (Weijters et al., 2010). We decided against including additional questionnaires with other response formats to ensure a sufficient sample size for each version.

Statistical Analysis

All analyses for our main study were conducted in R version 4.5.3 (2026-03-11). A full list of software versions can be found in Appendix C. The data were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis with the package lavaan (Rosseel, 2012). We used the weighted least squares, mean and variance adjusted (WLSMV) estimator, treating the questionnaire items as ordinal and the self-reported physical gold-standard items body height, body weight, and age as continuous variables. First, we specified one-factor models with no error correlations and with correlated errors for each trait. In both models, the gold-standard items and the other 12 items were specified as indicators of a single latent variable. Second, to test whether an interpretable latent variable remains after controlling for the gold-standard item and gender, one-factor models were specified with a single latent variable, with the questionnaire items additionally predicted by the gold-standard item and gender. 2 Third, to compare the correlations between the latent variables of the physical traits with the correlations between the gold-standard items, one full three-factor model without correlated errors was estimated, in which only the questionnaire items load on their respective latent variable, and correlations are estimated between the latent variables, between the gold-standard items, and between the latent variables and the gold-standard items.

We also conducted reliability analyses using the package MBESS (Kelley, 2023) and report McDonald's Omega as the reliability estimate of internal consistency for each scale. All analyses were run separately for both response formats (two-category and six-category scales).

The analyses reported in the current manuscript were not preregistered. However, the data we used have previously been analyzed in the first author's German dissertation (Eichhorn, 2019). As part of this dissertation, a preregistration was published at https://osf.io/cz3uv/?view_only=9cac02db231b48629fea9ae53c3038b9 2 Under the assumption that the gold-standard item closely represents the true physical trait, this analysis can be interpreted as a two-dimensional factor model where the latent variable is a second (psychological) factor independent of the physical trait (after controlling for gender). In our special case of investigating physical traits, we would argue that this analysis is more informative about the dimensionality of the scales than (a more common) exploratory factor analysis.

https://osf.io/cz3uv/?view_only=9cac02db231b48629fea9ae53c3038b9. The preregistration describes the planned data collection procedures and sample sizes, specifies the scale construction process, including the cognitive interviews and item selection based on the pilot sample, and registers the design of the questionnaires used in the validation sample, including the response format of both versions. In the current manuscript, we performed all of these steps as preregistered. However, our statistical analyses deviated from those listed in the preregistration. The reason for this deviation is that our general understanding of what we can learn from scales of physical traits about the construction of psychological scales has evolved continuously since preregistration, and we deem the analyses in the current manuscript more elegant for presenting our ideas than the originally preregistered analyses. In fact, the preregistration did not include the concept of gold-standard items or the detailed assumptions discussed in this manuscript. Instead, the registered research question was kept vague: "The main research question is how well the items represent the real score values.

More precisely, is it possible to construct a questionnaire, following the best practice of test construction, to measure a variable that we claim to measure." The results of the preregistered analyses are fully reported in Eichhorn (2019). Note that no results in this manuscript are in conflict with any of the preregistered analyses. Both the current manuscript and the preregistration state that all analyses should be considered exploratory.

Participants

The total sample of our main study consisted of 1854 participants aged between 18 and 97 years (M = 32.70, SD = 16.01), including 1036 women (56%) and 818 men (44%). The overall sample consisted of two independent subsamples, which were divided into the conditions with two (𝑁 = 921) and six (𝑁 = 933) response categories.

Participants were recruited in trains, colleges, universities, adult education centers, fitness studios, and various public places in Germany and Austria in November and December 2017.

Participation was voluntary and without reimbursement. Each participant was given a piece of paper informing them about the voluntary and anonymous nature of their participation, the purpose of the study, and the data to be collected. Upon providing consent, participants received one of two paper-and-pencil questionnaire versions: one using the two-category and the other using the six-category response scale. The two versions were alternated as questionnaires were handed out to participants. When a participant returned the questionnaire, the facilitator immediately checked for missing values and, if any were found, politely asked the participant to complete the missing questions. With this procedure, we achieved complete responses for all questionnaires.

No power analysis was performed to determine the sample size of the main study.

Instead, the goal was to collect at least 500 subjects per response format condition over a period of six weeks. No data was analyzed before data collection ended. The final sample size of our main study is typical of those used in current validation studies that publish diagnostic results.

According to Goretzko et al. (2024), the sample sizes used in typical validation studies in the journal Psychological Assessment from 2015 to 2020 were as follows: about 38 percent used sample sizes of 401 to 1000, and 25 percent sample sizes larger than 1000.

Table 1 shows the distribution of age, gender, level of education, and native language for each response format. As a result of the allocation procedure, the two subsamples are very similar. Due to the left-skewed age distribution and outlier values, we report both the mean and the median. Note. 𝑆𝐷 = standard deviation; 𝐼𝑄𝑅 = interquartile range.

Results

Assumption 1: The gold-standard item for body height, weight, and age should have the highest loading on its latent variable.

Table 2 displays the measurement models for the three scales for body height, body weight, and age for two and six response categories each. Overall, both response formats produced very similar loading patterns, but scales with two response categories yielded slightly higher loadings than scales with six response categories for most items. All model fits were within the expected range for psychological questionnaires (Goretzko et al., 2024). 3 Questionnaires with two response categories showed slightly better fit than those with six categories with respect to the CFI and the RMSEA, but slightly worse fit with respect to the SRMR. The best model fit was observed for the psychological scales for body height and weight with two response categories.

For the body height scales, the self-reported physical height loaded higher or similarly high on the latent variable compared to the questionnaire items. 4 However, this pattern differed for the weight and age scales, where several items loaded substantially higher on the latent variable than the physical items: For weight, the items 4 ("I am obese.") and 5 ("I weigh a lot.") had especially high loadings on the latent variable for both questionnaire versions, as did item 7 ("I have already lived most of my life.") for age.

The loading pattern for the weight and age scales, with lower loadings for the gold-standard items, suggests that these scales do not measure the intended constructs of physical weight and physical age. Even after allowing for correlated errors as suggested by standard modification indices, the loading patterns did only slightly improve (see Appendix B; physical height now also has the highest estimated loading with two response categories). Loading patterns with and without modifications were correlated at .98 (p < .001; absolute loadings pooled across all models, including the gold-standard items).

Assumption 2: The measurement should have a systematic psychological component, and an interpretable latent variable should remain after correcting item responses for the gold-standard items and gender.

Table 3 displays item loadings on the latent variable when controlling for the selfreported physical item and self-reported gender. Latent = standardized item loading on the respective latent variable (height, weight or age); Physical = standardized regression weight, predicting the item response by the respective selfreported physical measures (height, weight or age); Gender = standardized regression weight, predicting the item response by the self-reported gender (positive values imply higher item responses for men).

For body height, we obtained low item loadings on the latent variable but high regression weights with the gold-standard item of physical body height. In particular, the third item ("Chairs and tables are usually too low for me.") exhibited the highest loading on the latent variable for both response formats. In contrast, item 11 ("I have to stand at the front of group photos so that I can be seen clearly.") and item 12 ("When I hug other people in greeting, I have to bend downwards.") were best predicted by the self-reported physical body height for both response formats. 5 The absolute values of loadings on the latent variable were highly similar (close to .3) for all items. While this pattern would be consistent with the existence of a psychological latent height component that weakly contributes to the item responses after controlling for the selfreported physical item and gender, the loading pattern did not provide any indication of what this variable might represent.

For body weight, items with high loadings on the latent variable also exhibited strong associations with the self-reported physical body weight. Item 4 ("I am obese.") had the highest loading on the latent variable for both response formats. Item 5 ("I weigh a lot.") was explained best by the self-reported physical body weight. Item 9 ("I have a lot of space between the armrests in airplane seats.") had a low loading on the latent variable but was moderately predicted by the self-reported physical body weight for both response formats. Notably, item 11 ("If I have the choice between the elevator and the stairs, I take the elevator.") was not related to either the self-reported physical item or the latent variable for both response formats, indicating that it may represent a more health-related attitude.

Taken together, the resulting psychological latent weight component seems hard to interpret.

For age, we observed the biggest discrepancy between items with high loadings on the latent variable and items best predicted by self-reported physical age. Item 3 ("I have a lot of life experience.") and item 9 ("I have years of work experience.

") did not load on the latent variable after controlling for physical age and gender but were predicted by self-reported physical age for both response formats. In contrast, the three items most prototypical of the latent variable were item 2 ("Over time, my mental capacity has decreased."), item 4 ("Over time, my ability to react has decreased."), and item 5 ("Over time, my memory has deteriorated.") for both response formats. Thus, the psychological latent age component might be interpreted as mental age, but not all items load substantially on this general factor.

When examining self-reported gender, there were moderate standardized regression weights for some body height items (e.g., item 8 "Pants are often too short for me.") and body weight items (e.g., item 6 "I need to lose weight."). These items may pose problems when applied to both men and women (differential item functioning; see Hilbert et al., 2022, for a comparable case). Notably, standardized regression weights for self-reported gender predicting age items were mostly low.

Assumption 3a, b: The correlation pattern among the latent variables of the physical traits should match the correlation among the gold-standard items (3a). For scales with six response categories, reliability estimates should be higher, and correlations among latent variables and among gold-standard items should be more closely aligned.

As shown in Table 4, the correlations among the latent variables do not match the correlations among the self-reported physical items. Only height and age showed relatively similar correlations among latent variables and among physical items. However, the correlations between physical weight and physical age were overestimated by the correlations between the latent variables of weight and age, and the correlations between physical height and physical weight were underestimated by the correlations between the latent variables of height and weight. Most notably, correlations did not differ systematically between the questionnaires with two and with six response categories. Descriptively, the latent correlations seemed to reproduce the physical correlations slightly better for the questionnaires with two response categories.

However, reliability estimates (Omega) were lower for two response categories compared to six response categories. Note. Correlations among the latent variables are shown above the diagonal (in bold), and correlations among the self-reported physical measures are shown below the diagonal. For each response format, the reported correlations were obtained from a latent variable model that included all self-reported physical items and all latent variables with their assigned items. The models showed the following fit: scaled chi-square (six response categories) = 4,357.86, 𝑑𝑓 = 690, 𝑝 < .001, scaled CFI = .90, scaled RMSEA = .08, SRMR = .09; scaled chi-square (two response categories) = 2,098.37, 𝑑𝑓 = 690, 𝑝 < .001, scaled CFI = .93, scaled RMSEA = .05, SRMR = .10.
