Discussion

Summary

The goal of this study was to evaluate newly constructed psychological scales using goldstandard items. To achieve this, we focused on the specific setting of physical traits (i.e., body height, body weight, and chronological age), where theoretically robust gold-standard items are available in the form of numerical self-reports. Using confirmatory factor analysis, we found that, contrary to our assumptions, even in this ideal setting, gold-standard items did not exhibit the highest loadings on their corresponding latent variables for all physical traits. After controlling for the gold-standard item and gender, we observed a residual psychological component for all traits, but the interpretation of this latent variable was not straightforward. The correlations between the latent variables also did not closely match those between the goldstandard items. All results were highly similar across questionnaire versions with two and six response categories, although reliability estimates were slightly lower for the two-category versions.

Gold-Standard Items for Physical Traits

Despite the favorable setting when constructing psychological scales for physical traits and our carefully curated scale-construction process, gold-standard items did not fully function as expected with respect to our theoretical assumptions. Only on one of six scales (three physical traits measured via two response-scale versions each) did the gold-standard item exhibit a higher loading on the latent variable than the psychological items. That was on the six-category scale for body height, but not on the two-category version. Considering both the size and the measurement uncertainty of the factor loadings, it seems evident that the gold-standard items for weight and age loaded substantially lower on the latent variable than the best items of the respective scales. This finding raises questions about whether our psychological scales for weight and age accurately measure the physical traits they were designed to assess. Given this ambiguous construct validity, we would have expected the psychological items to capture a latent component beyond the physical trait itself. To examine this possibility, we conducted follow-up analyses controlling item responses for the gold-standard item and gender. However, the resulting residual latent variables proved difficult to interpret, both in terms of whether such a latent variable was present at all and how it could be meaningfully characterized (to further probe this issue, we also inspected the largest correlated errors in the one-factor models reported in Table B1, but without gaining additional insights). This lack of clarity is consistent with prior work suggesting that psychological questionnaires targeting physical attributes do not necessarily reflect a well-defined psychological construct that guides behavior (Hilbert et al., 2022; Van der Linden, 2016). A more detailed inspection revealed that this pattern varied across traits, but did not yield a coherent interpretation overall. For age, we found some indication that the residual latent variable may reflect cognitive or psychological age (Barak & Schiffman, 1981), as the highest-loading items all referred to mental decline. However, many age items showed negligible loadings, and the items tended to be either well predicted by the physical age item or strongly related to the residual latent variable, but rarely both. For weight, in contrast, items with high loadings on the residual factor were also substantially predicted by the physical item, suggesting no clear separation between physical and psychological components. For height, all items were well predicted by the physical item and showed small, relatively uniform residual loadings, providing some evidence for an additional latent dimension. However, the loading pattern did not indicate how this dimension could be interpreted. Taken together, these findings provide no consistent support for a meaningful psychological latent variable beyond the assessed physical traits of body height and weight. This interpretation is further reinforced by the mismatch between the correlations among the latent variables and those among the corresponding goldstandard items. 6 Overall, only the height scales performed close to expectations, and we therefore consider them the only appropriate measures of their respective physical trait.

In light of these issues, we sought to rule out the possibility that certain decisions in our questionnaire construction process introduced idiosyncratic problems 7 by comparing our results with those of Bortolotti et al. (2013), who applied a similar procedure with 27 items and two response categories to examine a gold-standard item for body height. They found a correlation of .86 between the estimated person parameter from a two-parameter logistic model and selfreported height, which closely matches our correlation between the gold-standard height item and the latent variable (two response categories: .87, six response categories: .86). The comparison does not suggest that our scales have unique problems, as we were able to conceptually replicate Bortolotti et al. (2013) with our independently developed questionnaire.

It is also noteworthy that our results were surprisingly robust across different response formats, with very similar findings for questionnaire versions with two and six response categories. We used a six-category response format to align with literature advising against the use of a middle category (Bradley et al., 2015; Masuda et al., 2017), and a two-category format because it is commonly used in symptom questionnaires within clinical psychology and medicine (Clark & Watson, 2019; Rosellini & Brown, 2021). As expected, reliability estimates were slightly higher for scales with six response categories than for those with two (Preston & Colman, 2000). However, the results for model fit and validity were mixed. Some fit indices suggested a slightly better fit for items with two response categories and some for six categories (although the differences were rather small). The same holds true for the differences between the correlations among the gold-standard items and the correlations among the latent variables.

Except for reliability, our results do not clearly favor either two or six response categories. While we would not expect substantially different results for scales with five or seven response categories, we cannot generalize our results to response formats that include a middle category (we only used formats without a middle category) or to response formats where all categories are labeled (we only labeled the endpoints). Hilbert et al. (2016 Hilbert et al. ( , 2022) ) showed that the same items, 7 For example, one reviewer questioned why many of our items use quite extreme item wording (e.g., "I have already lived most of my life") and pondered whether this might explain why our scales did not work as expected. However, our cognitive interviews and pilot study suggested that -maybe surprisingly -these items worked best to assess height, weight or age.

when measured with different numbers of response categories, do not necessarily measure the same latent variable. Thus, the selection of the response format may affect validity, prompting us to advise questionnaire developers to carefully consider the number of response categories when constructing psychological scales. An intensive cognitive pretesting phase can help clarify how respondents use and understand the categories, and empirical studies can help determine the number of response categories that provide better validity, reliability, and/or factor structures (Willis & Artino, 2013). In the current study, cognitive interviews and final results suggest that both applied response formats performed reasonably well.

Gold-Standard Items for Psychological Traits

Based on our findings from using gold-standard items to evaluate psychological scales for physical traits, we want to discuss whether a similar strategy could also be used in the more common task of constructing psychological scales for psychological traits, where theoretically strong gold-standard items are more difficult to identify.

In psychology, we try to use precise names for our latent variables, such as emotional intelligence, self-efficacy, conscientiousness, or narcissism. It might, therefore, seem straightforward to turn these construct labels into corresponding "gold-standard" items. But is it reasonable to expect that, in a questionnaire that measures narcissism, an item such as "I am a narcissist." (see Konrath, 2014) most accurately reflects the construct and, consequently, shows the highest factor loading? This question is closely related to psychological research on singleitem measures, that is, the measurement of psychological constructs using a single question in a rating-scale format, which often uses slightly longer wording and provides additional context in its instructions. Single-item measures are increasingly used in psychological research when constructs are narrowly defined and when there are strong practical reasons that longer multiitem scales cannot be applied without problems (Fuchs & Diamantopoulos, 2009). However, rigorous validation is repeatedly emphasized as equally important for single-item measures as for all psychological scales (Allen et al., 2022). In this literature, a common approach to assessing the validity of a newly constructed single-item measure is to examine its loading in a one-factor model that includes both the single-item measure and the items from an established multi-item scale for the same psychological construct (Fisher et al., 2016; Matthews et al., 2022). This is exactly the same logic we used in our study of gold-standard items for physical traits.

Thus, when constructing a new psychological scale, researchers could check whether a validated single-item measure of the same psychological construct is available and, if so, use it as a natural candidate for a gold-standard item in their validation study. Although it is argued that a good single-item measure should load highly on the latent variable shared with the multi-item scale, it is not required for the single-item measure to have a loading equal to or higher than those of the best items in the scale (Fisher et al., 2016; Matthews et al., 2022). We would argue that in most circumstances, it would nonetheless suggest issues with the newly constructed scale if the single-item measure has a low loading compared to the other items. Empirical evidence suggests that such analyses can detect problems in a substantial number of scale-construction processes. In Fisher et al. (2016), eight out of 18 newly constructed single-item measures had lower loadings than all items of the corresponding multi-item scale, and one single-item measure had a low absolute loading under 0.3. In Matthews et al. (2022), seven out of 91 newly developed single-item measures did not even load significantly on the factor shared with the corresponding multi-item scale, loaded in the wrong direction, or had a low absolute loading under 0.3. 8 Even if there is no consensus on how high the single-item measure's loading should be (Allen et al., 2022), most experts would agree that, in the cases reported above, there must be a problem with the single-item measure, the multi-item scale, or both.

What plausible reasons might explain why a single-item measure does not exhibit the highest loading relative to items from a corresponding multi-item scale? Prior research suggests that single-item measures are most effective when the underlying psychological construct is narrow in scope and low in complexity (Fuchs & Diamantopoulos, 2009; Matthews et al., 2022).

For such homogeneous constructs, it is comparatively easy to formulate an item that captures the construct's core meaning and is interpreted consistently across respondents. From this perspective, our application of constructing psychological scales for physical traits such as height, weight, and age should have provided particularly favorable conditions. In contrast, more heterogeneous and complex constructs, such as personality traits, are inherently more difficult to capture with a single item without introducing ambiguity. Although it has been argued that highly abstract single-item measures may still be useful for such constructs, especially when it is impractical to cover each content facet with an item (Fuchs & Diamantopoulos, 2009), any single-item measure in this context reflects a specific weighting of the construct's multiple aspects. Consequently, a single-item measure can be expected to show the highest loading only if the aspect it emphasizes is also the dominant component in the corresponding multi-item scale.

More generally, if a construct is sufficiently heterogeneous that no single item can be expected to dominate, it is questionable whether a unidimensional latent variable model is appropriate in the first place, as multiple factors and/or correlated errors are likely. In sum, we concur with prior literature that one should not assume that a single-item measure will necessarily exhibit the highest loading when combined with items from a corresponding multi-item scale. Instead, researchers should carefully compare the construct definitions underlying the multi-item scale and the single-item measure prior to validation. Such a theoretical analysis allows for the formulation of more informative expectations regarding the magnitude of the single-item loading than the minimal assumption that it merely differs from zero.

But what can be done in practice if no validated single-item measure closely matches the construct definition of a newly constructed scale? Can a gold-standard item still be defined in a broader sense? We argue that there are many settings in which this is both feasible and informative. Consider, for example, the measurement of personality using adjectives. Suppose we aim to assess the latent variable interpersonal warmth with items such as affectionate, friendly, talkative, unprejudiced, each rated on a scale from not at all (1) to fully and entirely (6) with six response categories. If these items indeed capture interpersonal warmth, they should also correlate with the adjective warm measured using the same response format. More importantly, one might question the construct definition itself if this straightforward item does not exhibit the highest loading in a one-factor model when included alongside the other items. In such cases, it is plausible that a different construct is being measured, for instance, friendliness, if the item friendly shows the highest loading. In this sense, the item warm can serve as a natural gold-standard item, analogous to the role of gold-standard indicators in our example involving physical traits. This raises the further question of whether such an item should be included in the final scale. We would argue that this decision depends on the specific research context and cannot be resolved in general terms. If the scale was originally intended to include an item directly reflecting the construct label (e.g., warm), its inclusion would be conceptually straightforward.

However, even if this were not the case, the structure of adjective-based questionnaires makes it difficult to justify omitting the most direct representation of the construct from empirical consideration. Ultimately, the decision of whether such items are retained as part of the final scale or used solely for validation purposes remains a matter of researcher judgment. Future studies should investigate different strategies of finding gold-standard items in more detail. For example, we are interested in using digital behavioral indicators from mobile sensing (Schoedel et al., 2026; Schoedel & Mehl, 2024) to validate scales with behavior-based definitions like some personality facets.

Despite these examples, we acknowledge that there will be many instances in which new psychological scales are constructed when theoretically strong gold-standard items are not available, and our suggested evaluation strategy cannot be readily applied. This should not be a problem, as it does not, in theory, invalidate the settings already discussed in which the strategy is meaningful. It is important to note that our evaluation strategy using gold-standard items is only a special case of a more general principle in test construction: Whenever constructing a new psychological scale, researchers should use their theoretical knowledge of the intended construct, its nomological network, and the scale's intended practical use cases to generate hypotheses about the scale and its items that are at least partly open to empirical testing. The more hypotheses about a new scale are available and the stronger the theoretical rationale for expecting a certain pattern, the more holistically researchers can empirically evaluate whether they actually measure the intended construct, and the better they should be able to convince the scientific community that they have constructed a useful new scale. Assessing the loadings of self-postulated gold-standard items is just one small example of such a hypothesis, and how convincing that hypothesis is will always depend on the concrete example.

Given that we did not consistently manage to construct scales in which gold-standard items had the highest factor loadings, even under the optimal setting of physical traits, we expect it to be even more difficult to achieve the theoretically desirable loading pattern when constructing scales for psychological traits. Nevertheless, we still think that gold-standard items can be a very useful tool for validating new psychological scales.

General Lessons and Recommendations

Despite following a rigorous, best-practice questionnaire construction process, our inability to construct valid psychological scales for physical traits that fully met our self-imposed criteria adds to a growing body of work highlighting the limitations of standard scaleconstruction approaches (Goretzko et al., 2020; Hilbert et al., 2016 Hilbert et al., , 2022;; Pargent et al., 2019).

Taken together, these findings call for critical reflection on common practices in item construction. We summarize our main insights below.

First, the choice of an optimal response format appears less clear-cut than often assumed (e.g., Lee & Paek, 2014). In the present study, items with only two response categories were not clearly inferior, despite common concerns in the literature. Although our binary scales showed lower reliability (as expected, based on Preston & Colman, 2000; Revilla et al., 2014), we observed no consistent disadvantages in terms of validity or model fit. This highlights that reliability reflects measurement precision, not validity. This does not necessarily contradict attempts to select items based on reliability (e.g., see Zijlmans et al., 2019) since items must have high loadings to achieve high reliability estimates for the scale. However, because reliability is easier to control for by adding more suitable items, construct validity seems to be the stronger argument when choosing the number of response categories. We therefore argue that decisions about response formats should be guided primarily by considerations of validity. In practice, this requires empirical comparison of alternative response formats, especially in high-stakes contexts such as clinical assessment or personnel selection. Importantly, the number of response categories may affect the latent variable being measured (Hilbert et al., 2016 (Hilbert et al., , 2022)), making such comparisons essential.

At the same time, all items should undergo thorough cognitive pretesting including the response format. Cognitive interviews or standardized pretesting frameworks (Gehlbach & Brinkworth, 2011; Wolf et al., 2025) can help ensure that respondents understand item wording and response options as intended, identify categories that are systematically overlooked, and assess the cognitive demands imposed by the questionnaire (Tourangeau et al., 2000). This is particularly relevant given that simpler formats, such as binary scales, may reduce respondent burden (Hilbert et al., 2016).

Second, overall model fit should not be overinterpreted as evidence of item quality. Good model fit does not guarantee that items are well formulated or substantively meaningful. Even when best-practice guidelines are followed during item construction, the resulting models may not outperform those in which items were purposely constructed in violation of such rules (Goretzko et al., 2020; Pargent et al., 2019). In the present study, even the a priori most suitable gold-standard items did not consistently exhibit the highest loadings. Thus, relying solely on statistical criteria, such as factor loadings, to evaluate items is insufficient. Instead, item selection should always consider both statistical performance and substantive content.

Finally, we emphasize the central importance of content validity in scale development.

Using gold-standard items (i.e., items for which high loadings are theoretically expected) represents a special case of a broader strategy: formulating explicit hypotheses about the role and behavior of individual items in a newly constructed scale. Such hypotheses may concern, for example, the ranking of factor loadings or the pattern of correlations with construct-divergent measures. Incorporating these expectations into the validation process can yield stronger, more informative tests of whether a scale adequately captures the intended latent variable.

For readers particularly interested in absolute model fit, we also report dynamic fit index cut-offs (McNeish, 2023) for the one-factor models of height, weight, and age for two and six response categories in our electronic supplemental materials (ESM A). Also note that our combination of the number of items per scale, the number of response categories for the ordinal scale, the final sample sizes, and the loading strengths is comparable to the most optimistic simulation conditions in McNeish (2023), in which even the traditional cut-offs work reasonably well when combining all three fit indices (see their Tables2 and 3).

Note that comparing point (or interval) estimates of factor loadings is not equivalent to a formal hypothesis test testing whether the true loadings of the gold-standard item are higher than all other loadings. Because our study is not confirmatory, we see no added value in computing and reporting such hypothesis tests, which is not trivial and would unnecessarily complicate our presentation of results. To give interested readers a better intuition about the plausible ranges of true factor loadings and the measurement uncertainty in our estimates, we provide 95% confidence intervals for all factor loadings from Table2in our electronic supplementary materials (ESM A).

Note that although in the model for height with two categories (controlling for the physical item and gender) the absolute standardized regression weights of the physical item predicting items 11 and 12 were estimated to be greater than one, this does not indicate a problem with the model. All models converged and the diagnostics used by the lavaan package(Rosseel, 2012) did not report any issues. In these models, each item is predicted by three variables (latent variable, physical item, gender). Thus, the standardized (partial) regression weights cannot be interpreted as correlations and do not have to fall within the [-1,1] range.

One reviewer raised the question whether measurement error in the self-reported physical items could explain the reported mismatch in the correlation pattern. In our adult population, we would expect reporting error to be negligible for age and small for height, with greater potential for reporting inaccuracies in weight. Such error could contribute to some discrepancies. However, this does not explain the pattern that the observed correlation between weight and height was substantially smaller for the latent variables than for the physical items. If the physical weight items were strongly affected by measurement error, the true correlation between the physical traits should be even higher than the correlation we observed between the physical items.

Unfortunately,Matthews et al. (2022) do not report how often the single-item measure had the highest estimated loading compared to the items from the multi-item scale and it is not possible to extract this information from their paper or supplemental materials.
